content: The Pelotas birth cohort study defined overweight as a body mass index (BMI) at or above the 85th percentile for sexand age-specific values. Obesity was defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile combined with subscapular and triceps skinfold thicknesses at or above the 90th percentile. Victora (2006) investigated the impact of breastfeeding duration on overweight and obesity in 18-year-old boys from the Pelotas cohort. Overweight and obesity were defined using the same criteria as above. The level of evidence for these findings was rated as very low. Two studies, Robinson (2009) and Victora (2006), assessed body composition in children breastfed into their second year compared to those breastfed for shorter durations. No significant differences in body composition were observed between these groups. Caleyachetty (2013) examined skinfold thickness in 5-year-old children based on breastfeeding duration, reporting geometric means for unadjusted data across three categories: 6–12 months, 12–17 months, and >18 months of breastfeeding. Six prospective cohort studies explored the association between infections in children and continued breastfeeding into the second year compared to shorter breastfeeding durations. These studies, primarily from high-income countries, analyzed infections such as gastrointestinal infections, respiratory tract infections, acute otitis media, and urinary tract infections. Christensen (2020) and Stordal (2017) documented the risk of hospitalization due to infections in children breastfed beyond one year compared to shorter durations. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Four studies provided data on the risk of respiratory tract infections in children breastfed into the second year compared to shorter durations. Similarly, four cohort studies assessed the risk of acute otitis media with continued breastfeeding, with the certainty of evidence rated as very low. One study compared the number of gastroenteritis episodes based on breastfeeding duration. Three studies (Fall 2011, Izadi 2013, Blix 2017) examined diabetes outcomes in children and adolescents in relation to breastfeeding status during the second year of life. Wong (2018) reported no significant differences in blood glucose levels in 3–6-year-olds breastfed for 12–23 months versus 6–12 months. Subgroup analyses for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months revealed no significant associations with diabetes-related parameters. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Eight studies reported cardiometabolic outcomes in children, adolescents, and adults (ages 3–32 years) in relation to breastfeeding status into the second year compared to shorter durations. Two cross-sectional studies (Maguire 2013, Villamor 2000) examined the impact of continued breastfeeding during the second year on iron deficiency and anemia in children up to 5–6 years old. Clinical heterogeneity was noted due to differences in study settings (Canada and Tanzania) and populations. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. No studies provided data on child mortality, gut health, or microbiome in relation to breastfeeding beyond one year. Two cohort studies (Harvey 2009, Muniz 2015) investigated the effects of continued breastfeeding during the second year on bone health. Harvey (2009) assessed outcomes at 4 years of age, while Muniz (2015) followed two birth cohorts, assessing one at 18 years and another at 30 years. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Thirteen cross-sectional studies and eight cohort studies from various countries examined the impact of breastfeeding continuation during the second year on oral health, specifically dental caries. The age of children at assessment ranged from 6 months to 12 years. Substantial heterogeneity was observed in terms of age, outcome definitions, and socioeconomic settings. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Nine studies (seven cross-sectional and two cohort) investigated the association between continued breastfeeding during the second year and asthma or allergies. The age of children assessed ranged from 2 to 15 years. No significant increase in asthma odds was observed with continued breastfeeding. Four studies examined the association of breastfeeding continuation with allergies, eczema, and hay fever, with no consistent findings. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Eight studies (seven cohort and one case-control) analyzed the association between breastfeeding continuation during the second year and breast cancer risk in women. All studies were from high-income countries, with most participants from urban or mixed settings. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Three cohort studies examined ovarian cancer risk, while one study each assessed cervical and uterine cancer risks. Two cohort studies analyzed the association of cumulative breastfeeding duration with lung cancer risk. The certainty of evidence for all cancer-related outcomes was rated as very low. Sixteen studies (eight cohort and eight cross-sectional) investigated the association between breastfeeding duration and maternal diabetes or blood glucose levels. Most participants were from high-income or upper-middle-income countries, with ages ranging from 19 to 81 years. Clinical heterogeneity was noted in terms of outcome definitions and adjusted parameters. Five studies specifically examined the association of breastfeeding duration per child with diabetes, while eleven studies analyzed cumulative breastfeeding duration. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low.
